note: Evidence examples (9 -> 18): two per capability, one conceptual and one applied. Draft for review.

capabilities.statement: Recognise creativity as a developable skill, related to critical thinking

evidence.title: Spotting everyday creativity in your own studying
evidence.example: You read a short account of Kaufman and Beghetto's (2009) Four C model, which ranges from mini-c (personal insights while learning) to Big-C (eminent creativity). You then note three mini-c moments from your own week and the critical judgement that went with each (for example, a new way of laying out biology revision notes that you then tested). This shows you see creativity as a skill you can develop, linked to critical thinking.
evidence.artefact: A short reflective log listing three mini-c moments, each with the idea, how you judged it and what happened.
grounding: model: Four C model of creativity (Kaufman and Beghetto 2009)

evidence.title: Improvement idea suggested in a part-time café job
evidence.example: In a part-time café job, you notice queues build at lunchtime and suggest a small change to how orders are taken. You describe how you came up with the idea and how you checked it would work before suggesting it (for example, a separate pre-order point for regular customers). This shows you treat creative thinking as part of everyday work, not a special talent.
evidence.artefact: A reflective log entry describing the idea, your checks and your supervisor's response to the suggestion.
grounding: professional: Treats creative thinking as part of professional practice, not a specialist's talent. (Vitae RDF A3: creativity)

genericOutcomes.title: Explaining why creativity counts as a buildable skill
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can explain why creativity functions as a skill that develops through practice rather than a fixed trait, linking it to critical thinking and judgement.
genericOutcomes.example: You set out, in your own words, why creativity should be treated as a skill that improves with practice rather than a fixed gift some people have and others do not. You link this to critical thinking by showing how judging and selecting among ideas is itself part of being creative, not separate from it. You give one example of your own thinking becoming more creative through deliberate practice over time.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short written explanation linking creativity's developability to critical judgement, with one personal example.
grounding: model: Four C model of creativity (Kaufman and Beghetto 2009)

genericOutcomes.title: Treating creative thinking as normal in any role
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can identify moments of creative thinking within everyday tasks and describe how judgement was used to decide whether an idea was worth pursuing.
genericOutcomes.example: Across a period of regular work, you keep a short record of moments when you generated an idea rather than simply following existing steps. For each one, you note what prompted the idea and how you judged whether it was worth pursuing. This builds a pattern across several entries, showing that you approach creative thinking as something expected of anyone doing the work, not a rare talent held by a specialist.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short record of several moments where an idea was generated and judged, kept over time.
grounding: professional: Approaches creative thinking as an expected part of any role, not a rare talent.

capabilities.statement: Use divergent and convergent thinking at the right stage of a task

evidence.title: Diverge then converge on a first-year design task
evidence.example: On a set design task, you separate idea generation from judgement, following the Double Diamond's diverge and converge phases (Design Council 2005) and Guilford's (1967) distinction between divergent and convergent thinking. You first list at least fifteen ideas without judging them, then apply stated criteria to choose one (for example, concepts for a low-cost water filter in a first-year engineering module). This shows you use each kind of thinking at the right stage.
evidence.artefact: Your unfiltered idea list, the criteria you set and a scored shortlist showing how you narrowed to one idea.

evidence.title: Choosing a fundraising event for a student society
evidence.example: As a member of a student society's fundraising team, you run a short session where members suggest as many event ideas as possible before anyone judges them. Then, with the group, you agree criteria such as cost and likely turnout and narrow to one event (for example, a charity quiz chosen from twenty ideas). This shows you generate options widely before narrowing to a decision.
evidence.artefact: Photographed idea sheets, the agreed criteria and the committee's note of the final decision.
grounding: professional: Generates options widely before narrowing to a decision. (Vitae RDF A3: creativity)

genericOutcomes.title: Showing staged thinking solve a complex problem
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can describe how divergent thinking to generate options and convergent thinking to select among them apply at different stages of solving a complex problem.
genericOutcomes.example: Faced with a problem that has no obvious single answer, you first open up as many possible approaches as you can without ruling any out, then switch deliberately to narrowing them down against stated criteria. You label which stage you are in at each point and explain why you moved from one to the other. This demonstrates applying critical thinking to a complex problem by identifying a creative and workable solution.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A labelled record showing the open stage, the narrowing stage and the reasoning for switching between them.

genericOutcomes.title: Widening then narrowing options to solve a live problem
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can identify the appropriate stage at which to widen a set of options before narrowing them against clear criteria to reach a workable solution.
genericOutcomes.example: Given a problem with several possible solutions and no obvious best answer, you first gather as many options as you can from those involved before ruling anything out. You then agree criteria with the group and use them to narrow the list to one recommended solution, recording why the others were set aside. This demonstrates applying critical thinking to a complex problem to reach a creative, workable solution.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short record of the options generated, the criteria agreed and the solution chosen with reasons.
grounding: professional: Generates options widely before narrowing to a decision. (Vitae RDF A3: creativity)

capabilities.statement: Overcome creative barriers such as fear of failure and perfectionism

evidence.title: Mindset reflection on sharing a rough draft
evidence.example: You choose a piece of work you would usually keep back until it felt perfect and share an early, rough version for feedback. Using Dweck's (2006) distinction between fixed and growth mindsets, you reflect on the thoughts that held you back and what the feedback taught you (for example, sharing an unfinished composition in a music workshop). This shows you can notice and work past fear of failure and perfectionism.
evidence.artefact: A reflective entry with the rough draft, the feedback received and your account of how you handled the urge to hold back.

evidence.title: Trying a new classroom activity on school placement
evidence.example: On a primary school placement, you try a new activity you have not seen modelled, knowing it might not work. It partly fails, and you record what happened, what you learned and how you would adapt it, rather than going back to safe methods (for example, a role-play to teach fractions that ran over time). This shows you put forward and test ideas without fear of early failure.
evidence.artefact: Your lesson plan and evaluation for the activity, with your placement mentor's signed observation comments.
grounding: professional: Puts forward and tests ideas without fear of early failure. (Vitae RDF A3: creativity)

genericOutcomes.title: Explaining how perfectionism was overcome to apply an idea
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can explain how fear of failure and perfectionism inhibit creative action, and describe reasoning that helps move past such barriers.
genericOutcomes.example: You identify a point where perfectionism, or a fear of getting it wrong, nearly stopped you from trying out an idea. You explain the thinking that was holding you back, the reasoning you used to move past it, and the small step you took to test the idea despite the risk of it not working. This demonstrates showing creativity in applying an idea rather than withholding it until it felt entirely safe.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short written account of the barrier noticed, the reasoning used to move past it and the step taken.

genericOutcomes.title: Testing an early idea despite the risk of it failing
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can identify an early, imperfect idea worth testing in practice and describe how to proceed despite the risk that it might not succeed.
genericOutcomes.example: Rather than waiting until an idea feels fully worked out, you put forward an early version of it and test it in practice, accepting that it might not work the first time. When it does not fully succeed, you record what you learned and adjust it rather than withdrawing the idea altogether. This demonstrates showing creativity and enterprise by applying an idea and working through its early setbacks.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short record of the early idea tested, what happened and the adjustment made afterwards.
grounding: professional: Puts forward and tests ideas without fear of early failure. (Vitae RDF A3: creativity)

capabilities.statement: Draw on creativity theory to justify a creative approach

evidence.title: Theory-based rationale for an unconventional project format
evidence.example: You propose an unconventional format for a project and justify it with theory. You use Anderson and Krathwohl's (2001) revised taxonomy, where create (generating, planning, producing) is the highest cognitive process, and de Bono's (1970) lateral thinking to explain how the format leads you to new connections (for example, presenting a geography project as an interactive story map instead of a report). This shows you draw on creativity theory to justify your approach.
evidence.artefact: A 600-word rationale citing both theories, attached to the project proposal and your tutor's approval.

evidence.title: Proposal for a new induction format at a leisure centre
evidence.example: Working part time at a leisure centre, you propose replacing the written induction for new staff with a short, hands-on walk-through. You explain your reasoning to your manager: what is not working now, why your idea is likely to help and how you would judge whether it did (for example, fewer safety questions from new starters in their first month).
evidence.artefact: Your written proposal, the evidence you gathered for it and your manager's reply.
grounding: professional: Explains the reasoning behind an innovative proposal.

genericOutcomes.title: Using theory to justify an unconventional approach
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can analyse an unconventional approach against an established creativity theory to justify why it is likely to produce a stronger outcome than convention.
genericOutcomes.example: You choose an unconventional way of approaching a piece of work and set out, with reference to established theory, why that choice is more likely to produce a strong result than a conventional one. You name the theory or model you are drawing on and explain precisely how it supports your reasoning, rather than treating the approach as simply a preference. This demonstrates showing creativity in applying an idea, backed by a stated rationale rather than instinct.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short written justification naming the theory used and linking it directly to the chosen approach.

genericOutcomes.title: Backing an innovative proposal with a stated rationale
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can justify an innovative proposal with a clear, step by step rationale that explains its advantage over current practice and how success would be checked.
genericOutcomes.example: When you put forward an idea that departs from how things are usually done, you do not rely on instinct alone. You set out your reasoning step by step: what the current approach lacks, why your alternative should work better, and how its success could be checked. This demonstrates showing creativity and enterprise in applying an idea, with a rationale that someone else could follow and question.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A written proposal with its stated rationale and a note of how success would be checked.
grounding: professional: Explains the reasoning behind an innovative proposal.

evidence.title: SCAMPER and creative problem-solving record on a product redesign
evidence.example: You work through a design problem using a structured method rather than waiting for inspiration. You follow Osborn's (1953) creative problem-solving process, deferring judgement while generating ideas, and use SCAMPER (Eberle 1971) prompts to vary an existing product (for example, redesigning a pill organiser for older users in a product design module). You record which prompts produced usable ideas and why you chose your final solution.
evidence.artefact: A method record showing the problem statement, ideas from each SCAMPER prompt, your selection criteria and the chosen concept.

evidence.title: Structured fix for a charity shop donation backlog
evidence.example: Volunteering at a charity shop where donations pile up unsorted, you use a structured method with the team: you define the problem, ask "why" repeatedly to reach its cause, generate options and trial one (for example, a sorting rota tied to delivery days). You measure whether the backlog falls. This shows you use structured methods to solve real problems and improve how things work.
evidence.artefact: A one-page problem-solving record with the cause analysis, options, trial results and the shop manager's comments.
grounding: professional: Uses structured methods to solve problems and design improvements. (Vitae RDF A3: creativity)

genericOutcomes.title: Applying a named method to reach a creative solution
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can apply a named structured method, defining a problem, generating options without early judgement, then selecting and refining one, to reach a creative solution.
genericOutcomes.example: Given a problem with no obvious solution, you choose a named structured method, rather than relying on unguided brainstorming, and follow its steps in order: defining the problem precisely, generating options without early judgement, then selecting and refining one. You record which step of the method produced your strongest option. This demonstrates applying critical thinking to a complex problem to identify a creative and workable solution.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A step-by-step record of the method followed, the options it produced and the solution selected.

genericOutcomes.title: Solving a complex problem through a structured method
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can apply a structured problem solving method to generate and test options against agreed criteria, recording whether the chosen solution resolved the original problem.
genericOutcomes.example: When a problem in your work has no quick fix, you follow a structured method rather than guessing at a solution: you define the problem, generate a wide set of options without ruling any out too early, then apply agreed criteria to choose and trial one. You record the outcome of the trial and whether it resolved the original problem. This demonstrates applying critical thinking to a complex problem to identify a creative, workable solution.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A written record of the method's steps, the options generated and the result of the trial.
grounding: professional: Uses structured methods to solve problems and design improvements. (Vitae RDF A3: creativity)

capabilities.statement: Shift approach when a strategy is not working (cognitive flexibility)

evidence.title: Double-loop review of a failing research strategy
evidence.example: When your dissertation data collection stalls, you write a review using Argyris and Schon's (1978) single-loop and double-loop learning. You record the first fixes you tried, then question the assumption behind your strategy and change approach (for example, a psychology study that moved from an online survey to short interviews after recruitment failed). This shows you can shift approach when a strategy is not working, and justify the change.
evidence.artefact: A strategy review note comparing single-loop and double-loop changes, with your supervisor's agreement to the revised method.
grounding: model: Single-loop and double-loop learning (Argyris and Schon 1978)

evidence.title: Adapting a coaching session that was not working
evidence.example: Coaching a junior football team as a volunteer, you notice partway through a session that a drill is not working: players are bored and the skill is not improving. You stop, change the format and record why (for example, swapping a queue-based passing drill for small-sided games). Afterwards you plan the next session differently. This shows you adapt your approach when results are not what you expected.
evidence.artefact: Your session plan with notes on the change made mid-session and a short review from the head coach.
grounding: professional: Adapts approach when circumstances or results change. (Vitae RDF B2: self-management)

genericOutcomes.title: Adjusting an approach once a gap in understanding appears
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can analyse how a mistaken assumption about the subject matter can undermine a planned approach, and explain how updated understanding should prompt a change of strategy.
genericOutcomes.example: While working through a task, you find that your planned approach relies on an assumption about the subject matter that turns out to be wrong. Rather than pressing on, you pause, update your understanding, and change your strategy to fit what you now know. You record the original assumption, what corrected it and the new strategy. This demonstrates a well-founded grasp of the subject's core content guiding a change in approach.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short note recording the original assumption, the correction and the revised strategy adopted.
grounding: model: Single-loop and double-loop learning (Argyris and Schon 1978)

genericOutcomes.title: Changing course once results reveal a misunderstanding
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can evaluate results that reveal a flawed approach, correct the underlying misunderstanding and adjust strategy accordingly rather than continuing regardless.
genericOutcomes.example: Partway through a task, results show that an approach based on your current understanding of the subject is not working as expected. Instead of continuing regardless, you revisit what you know, correct the gap and adjust your approach accordingly, recording both the original plan and the revised one. This demonstrates a well-founded grasp of the subject's core content being used to recognise and fix a flawed strategy.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short record contrasting the original approach, the misunderstanding found and the revised approach taken.
grounding: professional: Adapts approach when circumstances or results change. (Vitae RDF B2: self-management)

capabilities.statement: Apply creativity and enterprise thinking in professional contexts

evidence.title: Business Model Canvas for a venture idea from your discipline
evidence.example: You develop an idea from your own subject into a possible venture and test its logic with Osterwalder and Pigneur's (2010) Business Model Canvas. You fill each of the nine blocks with evidence, identify the weakest assumptions and revise the idea (for example, a computing student's app that helps students find quiet study spaces, revised after finding no one would pay for it).
evidence.artefact: A completed Business Model Canvas with evidence notes, the assumptions you tested and a revised version of the idea.
grounding: model: Business Model Canvas (Osterwalder and Pigneur 2010)

evidence.title: Live brief pitch to grow a theatre's young audience
evidence.example: On a live brief from a local theatre, your team is asked to find ways to attract more audience members aged 18 to 25. You identify an opportunity, develop it into a costed proposal and pitch it to the theatre's staff (for example, a student ticket scheme linked to post-show discussions). This shows you can apply creativity and enterprise thinking in a professional context.
evidence.artefact: The pitch deck, the costed proposal and the theatre's written feedback on the idea's value and feasibility.
grounding: professional: Identifies opportunities and turns ideas into value for an organisation or venture. (Vitae RDF A3: creativity; Vitae RDF D3: engagement and impact)

genericOutcomes.title: Showing creativity applied to a real opportunity
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can construct a reasoned case for a genuine opportunity, synthesising its likely beneficiaries, costs and success criteria, and justify a revision based on tested evidence.
genericOutcomes.example: You identify a genuine opportunity connected to an area you know well, and work through how you would turn it into something of value: who would benefit, what it would cost to develop and how you would know if it had succeeded. You test the weakest part of the idea with real evidence rather than assumption, and revise it in light of what you find. This demonstrates creativity and enterprise applied with discipline rather than left as a vague idea.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short written case for the opportunity, the weakest assumption tested and the resulting revision.
grounding: model: Business Model Canvas (Osterwalder and Pigneur 2010)

genericOutcomes.title: Turning an identified opportunity into a proposal of value
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can construct a costed proposal from an identified opportunity, present it for approval and justify any changes made in response to the feedback received.
genericOutcomes.example: You spot an opportunity within an organisation or venture you are involved with, and take it from idea to a proposal with a stated cost and expected benefit. You pitch it to those who would need to approve or fund it, and record their response, including any changes you would need to make. This demonstrates showing creativity and enterprise by applying an idea to create something of real value.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A written proposal with its costed benefit and a record of the response it received.
grounding: professional: Identifies opportunities and turns ideas into value for an organisation or venture. (Vitae RDF A3: creativity; Vitae RDF D3: engagement and impact)

capabilities.statement: Turn ideas into action under uncertainty

evidence.title: Effectuation plan for a pilot with an uncertain outcome
evidence.example: You plan a new initiative where the outcome cannot be predicted, using Sarasvathy's (2001) effectuation principles: start with the means you have, commit only what you can afford to lose, and build partnerships as you go. You record how you acted on the idea without waiting for certainty (for example, a social work student piloting a peer-support group for young carers with no data on likely demand).
evidence.artefact: An effectuation plan setting out your means, affordable loss and partners, with a log of decisions taken as things changed.

evidence.title: Launching a community repair café with unknown demand
evidence.example: With a local community group, you set up a monthly repair café without knowing whether anyone will come or which skills will be needed. You run a small first event, learn from it and adjust the next (for example, adding bike repairs after most visitors brought bicycles). This shows you can turn an idea into action under uncertainty and adapt as you learn.
evidence.artefact: An action log across three events with attendance figures, changes made and a short statement from the group's organiser.

genericOutcomes.title: Reasoning through acting on an idea before certainty exists
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can justify a deliberate decision to act on an idea before certainty exists, accounting for available resources, acceptable risk and a response to early setbacks.
genericOutcomes.example: You set out, step by step, how you decided to act on an idea despite not knowing whether it would succeed: what you already had available to use, how much you were prepared to risk, and what you would do if early signs were discouraging. You explain this as a deliberate way of managing uncertainty, not as guesswork. This demonstrates turning an idea into action under uncertainty through considered reasoning.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short written account of the resources used, the risk accepted and the plan if early signs were poor.
grounding: benchmark: none (unattributed; written from capability statement)

genericOutcomes.title: Committing to an initial step despite an unclear outcome
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can construct a limited first step on an idea under genuine uncertainty, treating its outcome as information that shapes the next decision rather than a final verdict.
genericOutcomes.example: Rather than waiting for enough certainty to guarantee success, you commit to a first, limited step on an idea, using only what you can afford to risk, and treat the result as information rather than a final verdict. You record what that first step taught you and how it changed your next move. This demonstrates turning an idea into action under uncertainty rather than delaying until the risk disappears entirely.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short record of the initial step taken, what it revealed and the next move it led to.
grounding: professional: Acts on an idea under genuine uncertainty and adapts it as real information comes in.
benchmark: none (unattributed; written from capability statement)

capabilities.statement: Own a creative practice, aware of one's own creative process

evidence.title: Creative process statement mapped to Wallas' stages
evidence.example: Over a major project, you keep notes on how your ideas formed, then write a statement analysing your own creative process using Wallas' (1926) four stages: preparation, incubation, illumination and verification. You identify where your process departs from the model and what conditions help you work at your best (for example, a master's chemistry student finding that breakthroughs came after stepping away from failed syntheses).
evidence.artefact: A creative process statement with dated project notes as evidence, plus the conditions and habits you now plan for.
grounding: model: Four-stage model of the creative process (Wallas 1926)

evidence.title: Professional creative practice portfolio from an industry placement
evidence.example: During an industry placement in a games studio, you build a portfolio that shows not only finished work but how you get to original ideas, the methods you rely on and the risks you choose to take. You discuss it with a senior practitioner and revise how you describe your practice (for example, how you prototype quickly before committing to a design).
evidence.artefact: A practice portfolio with a creative practice statement and a senior practitioner's written feedback on it.
grounding: practice: industry placement in a creative studio

genericOutcomes.title: Analysing your own creative process against a named model
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can critique their own creative process against a recognised stage model, identifying which stages are rushed or skipped and the implications for future work.
genericOutcomes.example: You examine how your own ideas tend to form, from first noticing a problem through to a finished piece of work, and compare this against a named stage model of the creative process. You identify which stages you move through quickly, which you tend to skip, and what that means for how you should plan future work. This demonstrates owning a creative practice through genuine awareness of your own process, not assumption.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A written comparison of your own process against the named model, with implications for future planning.
grounding: model: Four-stage model of the creative process (Wallas 1926)

genericOutcomes.title: Describing your own creative practice to someone experienced
genericOutcomes.learningOutcome: The student can construct an account of their own creative practice, including its triggers and risks, and justify revisions made after testing it against an experienced perspective.
genericOutcomes.example: You put into words how you actually go about producing original work: what triggers your ideas, the habits you rely on, and the risks you choose to take or avoid. You test this description against the view of someone experienced in similar work and revise it where their observations do not match your own account. This demonstrates owning a creative practice through active, checked awareness rather than unexamined habit.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A written practice statement, revised after discussion, with a note of what changed and why.
grounding: professional: Describes and refines an account of their own creative method, not only their finished output.
